### Library entrance closure: Monday to Thursday

The library’s east entrance, facing the bus shelter, will be closed to everyone from Monday through Thursday while the pavement immediately outside it is replaced. The library will remain open on its usual schedule. Please use the west entrance, which faces the playground.

If you are coming from the playground, use the west entrance as normal. If you are coming from the bus shelter, follow the signed path along the south side of the building to the west entrance. This route adds approximately 120 metres to the journey. It has no steps, but one section has a temporary firm mat over uneven ground. The mat is on the route to the west entrance. The east entrance remains closed, including to wheelchair users. You can still wait at the bus shelter, but the direct path from the shelter to the east entrance will be behind a temporary barrier.

During library opening hours, staff can meet visitors at the bus shelter and accompany them to the west entrance. If you would like this help, call the library desk before setting out. You can also request help on arrival by calling the number displayed at the shelter, although a staff member may not be available immediately. The library cannot provide transport around the building.

The returns slot beside the east entrance will also be inaccessible. Books due Monday through Thursday may be returned on Friday without a late charge, including books borrowed from another branch.

Heavy rain may delay the work. If the closure lasts longer, an updated notice will be posted at both entrances and at the bus shelter. The Friday return arrangement will remain in place unless that notice announces a further extension.

For the next six weeks, the reading room will keep its usual hours, but map retrieval from the archive will follow a new schedule. Requests received before noon with a shelfmark will be collected for retrieval at 2 p.m. There will be no second retrieval in the afternoon.

You do not need to arrive before noon. If you request a map in advance, you may arrive later. If you arrive without having requested a map, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves, and you may submit a request for the next opening day.

If your request does not include a shelfmark, staff will help identify the item. The request will be held until then and added to the next retrieval after identification, which may be on a later day.

Maps already identified as fragile need a support prepared by the conservation team. The team will contact you to arrange an appointment; these appointments are not part of the 2 p.m. retrieval. The catalogue will identify maps known to need support. If staff find during retrieval that another item needs support, they will contact you.

The trial aims to reduce interruptions in the store. Opening hours are unchanged. We will count delayed requests and review reader comments before deciding whether to continue. Comment cards will be available at the desk throughout the trial.

The amber indicator on the curing-line monitor appeared just after washdown on three of the last five morning shifts. It means the humidity probe’s reading is outside the range accepted by the controller, but it does not tell us whether the room is too humid or the probe’s reading is unreliable. The other display, often called the backup, measures temperature only. A normal reading there cannot resolve a question about humidity.

On all three mornings, the indicator cleared within twelve minutes. Operators wiped moisture from the outside of the probe housing on two mornings. On the third, nobody touched it. These observations are consistent with moisture around the housing, but they do not establish that wiping cleared the warning. The housing is not the sensing element, and this note records the wiping without recommending it as a remedy.

For now, record when the indicator appears, when it clears, and whether washdown has finished. Do not open the housing. If the indicator remains amber after fifteen minutes, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may request a handheld humidity check using the unit in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading does not give standing permission to restart. The shift lead must make that decision.

Maintenance has been asked to inspect the seal at the next planned stop, but the request does not establish that the seal has failed. Continue recording mornings when no warning appears, using the “no warning” box beside the time fields in the log. We need those records as well as warning records to determine how often the pattern occurs.

Does speaking the current row label help users return to a table after closing a note? We compared a prototype that gave this cue with an existing version that returned keyboard focus to the same cell without speaking. Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. Each set used different tables, and half the participants in each order group used the reverse table assignment.

The median of participants’ mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. These are two group medians, not the median of participants’ within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We measured time from closing the note to activating the requested table entry; reading the note was not timed. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test.

Nine participants said in the closing interview that the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of them also said it sometimes interrupted speech they were still listening to. The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit, but none asked to remove the feature. We did not ask whether they wanted it enabled by default.

The order and table assignments reduced the alignment between version and practice, but participants may still have carried a search strategy from the first set of tasks into the second. The study included experienced screen-reader users only. Its tables fit on one screen, so it does not establish how the cue would work with larger tables.

The results make an orientation benefit plausible for some users in these tasks. They also raise a design question: can the cue help users locate their place without interrupting speech they are listening to? An interruptible cue is one possible next version, but we did not implement or test it here. The timing results provide no evidence about that behavior.

We asked whether a spoken location cue helps screen-reader users return to a table after opening a note. In the prototype with the cue, closing a note spoke the current row label. The existing version returned keyboard focus to the same cell without speaking. Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. The tasks used different tables in each set, and half of each order group used the tables in the reverse version assignment.

The median of participants’ mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. This compares two group medians, not the median of participants’ within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We did not calculate a confidence interval or perform a significance test. Timing began when participants closed the note and ended when they activated the requested table entry; reading the note was not timed.

Nine participants said in closing interviews that the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of them also described times when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit. None asked to remove the feature, but participants were not asked whether they wanted it enabled by default.

What do these results tell us about the cue? They make an orientation benefit plausible for some users in these tasks, and they show that the cue can compete with ongoing speech. The timings alone do not establish whether the difference is reliable. Even if it is, the interruption remains a design concern. An interruptible cue could address that concern, but we did not implement or test that behavior, so these results provide no evidence about its effects.

The study reduced the complete alignment of version and practice by varying task order, but it could not rule out learning effects: participants may have carried a search strategy from the first set of tasks into the second. We recruited experienced screen-reader users, so we do not know how less experienced users would respond. The prototype’s tables fit on one screen, and the study does not establish performance on larger tables.

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\geq 0\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\geq 1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, this tail is less than any given \(\varepsilon>0\) once \(N\) is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\geq a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\geq 0\).

To understand the infinite series, we first add its first \(N\) terms. The intermediate terms cancel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the distance from \(S_N\) to \(a_1\) is
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to 0\) gives an integer \(K\geq 1\) such that
\[
0\leq a_k<\varepsilon\qquad\text{whenever }k\geq K.
\]
For every \(N\geq K\), we therefore have \(|S_N-a_1|<\varepsilon\). This proves that the partial sums converge to \(a_1\), which is precisely what
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1
\]
means.

Now fix \(N\geq 1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The distance between this finite tail sum and \(a_{N+1}\) is \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\) increases. Hence the infinite tail exists and equals
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
With \(K\) chosen above, every \(N\geq K\) satisfies
\[
0\leq \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

These calculations also cover equal consecutive terms, for which \(d_n=0\). If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n\) to be zero, and the same identities still apply. \(\square\)

\left|\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n-a_{N+1}\right|
=a_{M+1}\longrightarrow 0
\qquad\text{as }M\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

\[
a_k<\varepsilon\qquad\text{whenever }k\geq K.

\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.

The compost thermometer has returned from its brief career as a dibber. It is back on the hook inside the shed, where it can resume measuring temperature rather than making holes. Please use the wooden dibbers for planting. They have fewer opinions about heat.

This month we are comparing the middle of the active heap with its outer edge. On your rota day, take one reading at each marked position and record both on the sheet. Push the probe to the mark on its shaft, wait until the display settles, and wipe it before returning it to the hook. If the display never settles, write that down instead of choosing the number you like best.

A warmer middle is interesting, but a single pair of readings will not tell us whether the whole heap is ready to use. We are collecting observations over the month. The stewards will also inspect the material before deciding whether to open the bay for collection. Until the notice changes, please keep adding suitable material to the active bay and leave the resting bay alone.

The recording sheet has room for comments because weather, recently added material, and an uncooperative display may help explain a reading. You do not need to write a small novel. “Heavy rain this morning” is useful. “The heap has entered a troubled period” is less useful, though we appreciate the concern.
